name: Nikto – Web Server Fingerprinting
description: Nikto web scanner fingerprints the server, detects misconfigurations, outdated software, dangerous files, and default credentials. -Tuning b restricts to software identification only (fast, less noisy). Full scan (-Tuning 0123456789abcde) is comprehensive but loud.
notes: Tuning codes: b = Software Identification, 1 = Interesting Files, 2 = Misconfig, 4 = Info Disclosure, 9 = SQL Injection, a = Auth Bypass, c = XSS/Injection. Use -ssl for HTTPS targets. -output saves to file; -Format specifies format (txt/xml/html/csv). Nikto is not stealthy — generates many requests and is easily detected by WAFs/IDS. Run after wafw00f to understand detection risk.

defense.why_it_works: Nikto is an active web-server scanner that requests known files and paths to identify software and configuration. With -Tuning b it restricts to Software Identification modules — avoiding the noisiest vulnerability probes while still fingerprinting the server, CMS, and exposed files.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to the target web server (URL/host).
defense.impact: A technology profile: web-server and version (e.g. Apache 2.4.41, outdated), CMS (WordPress), the login page (/wp-login.php), disclosed files (license.txt), and missing security headers — each a CVE match or entry point.
defense.detection:
Active scanning: Nikto issues many requests for known files/paths, which appear in web access logs and are readily flagged by IDS/WAF (Nikto has a recognisable default user-agent and request signature). -Tuning b reduces volume but the traffic is still active and loggable.

[MITRE T1595.002] Vulnerability scanning checks whether a target's software and version align with a known exploit; the probing pattern is detectable in web/IDS logs.
defense.artifacts: A burst of requests for known paths/files (wp-login.php, license.txt, admin pages) in web access logs; Nikto's default user-agent string; WAF/IDS scan alerts.
defense.prevention:
Deploy a WAF and bot/scan detection; suppress server version/banner disclosure and remove or protect files such as license.txt; add the missing security headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options); rate-limit. Keep software patched so any disclosed version is not exploitable.

[MITRE T1595.002 M1056] Focus on minimising the amount and sensitivity of data exposed to external parties.
defense.evasion: -Tuning b limits Nikto to software-identification modules to cut noise; a custom user-agent and a slower request rate reduce signature- and rate-based detection.
defense.misconfiguration: Services expose excessive information: version banners, supported auth methods, valid usernames via error responses. IPMI has no authentication (version 2.0 cipher 0 vulnerability). RSH/rexec trust .rhosts files. rsync shares readable anonymously. Oracle TNS allows remote poisoning in older versions.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# IPMI cipher 0 — no authentication required:
# ipmitool -H <ip> -U admin -P '' -I lanplus -C 0 chassis status
# Returns valid data — auth bypassed entirely

# rsync anonymous access:
# rsync --list-only rsync://<ip>/  # lists all modules without auth
# rsync rsync://<ip>/backup /tmp   # downloads backup files

# Oracle TNS — version banner reveals exact version:
# nmap -p 1521 -sV -> Oracle Database 11.2.0.4 (exact version)
defense.secure_config:
# IPMI — disable cipher 0, enable only strong ciphers:
# /etc/ipmi/ipmievd.conf: IPMI_CIPHER_SUITE=17  (AES, mandatory auth)
# Or disable IPMI entirely if not needed (BMC IPMI = critical attack surface)

# rsync — require auth:
# /etc/rsyncd.conf:
# [backup]
#   auth users = backupuser
#   secrets file = /etc/rsyncd.secrets
#   hosts allow = 10.10.1.0/24

# RSH/rexec — disable entirely (replaced by SSH):
systemctl disable rsh.socket rexec.socket rlogin.socket

# Oracle TNS — disable remote admin, enforce auth:
# sqlnet.ora: SQLNET.AUTHENTICATION_SERVICES = (BEQ, TCPS)  (not NONE)
